question: Which pair of traversals always determines a binary tree with distinct values?
option_c: Level order and preorder without markers
explanation: Preorder identifies the root, and inorder splits the rest into left and right. Preorder + postorder fails whenever a node has a single child: 1→2 on the left and 1→2 on the right both give pre 1 2, post 2 1.

question: pre = 1 2 4 5 3 6 and in = 4 2 5 1 3 6. What is the postorder?
explanation: 1 is the root; 4 2 5 is its left part (root 2 with children 4 and 5) and 3 6 its right part (root 3 with right child 6). Postorder: 4 5 2 6 3 1.

question: Building from preorder + inorder by searching the inorder linearly for each root costs how much on a chain of n nodes?
explanation: Each of the n roots is searched for in a range of up to n elements. A value → index hash map makes each lookup O(1), so the build becomes O(n).

question: When building from postorder + inorder with one running index that walks the postorder from the end, which subtree must be built first?
explanation: Postorder read backwards is N R L, so after the root, the next values belong to the right subtree.

question: How many null markers does a preorder serialization with markers contain for a tree of n nodes?
explanation: There are 2n child slots and n − 1 are used by real nodes (every node except the root is someone's child), leaving n + 1 empty ones.

question: Why is this deserializer O(n²) on a chain?
option_a: Recursion with one call per node is always quadratic, whatever each call does
option_b: stoi scans the whole remaining string, so each token costs O(n) to parse
option_c: Each call copies the rest of the string: n + (n−1) + … characters in total
option_d: It is O(n): the copies are moved, not copied, so they cost nothing
explanation: Thread a shared read position (size_t& i) or a string_view through the calls instead of copying the remainder.

question: In build(pre, i, bound) for a BST preorder, the next value is not below bound. What happens?
option_a: It returns nullptr without consuming it: an ancestor will take it on its right side
option_b: It is inserted as the right child of the current node, because it is larger than the bound
option_c: The input cannot be a valid BST preorder, so the function should report an error
option_d: The value is skipped and the next one is tried, because it does not fit this subtree
explanation: Not consuming it is the key. Some ancestor whose bound allows it will take it as part of its right subtree. Each value is consumed exactly once, so the build is O(n).

question: Building the maximum binary tree with a monotonic stack, x arrives and pops several smaller nodes. Where do they go?
option_a: They are deleted, because a node smaller than a later value can never be in the tree
option_b: The last one popped becomes x's left child; the rest stay linked below it
option_c: The first popped node becomes the right child of x, and the others are pushed back
option_d: They are pushed again after x, so that the stack stays sorted for the next element
explanation: The popped nodes form a right-going chain of values smaller than x, and they lie to x's left in the array. Hanging the largest of them under x->left keeps that chain intact.

question: Why must null markers be included when testing "is sub a subtree of root" by searching for the serialization?
option_a: The markers make KMP faster, because the pattern gets a longer prefix function
option_b: They are optional: any traversal of distinct-shaped trees gives distinct sequences
option_c: Without them a match may cover only the top of a bigger subtree
option_d: They are needed to tell negative values apart from positive ones in the token stream
explanation: The markers under the pattern's leaves force the matching nodes in root to be leaves too, and they make the encoding a prefix code.

question: A tree arrives as unordered (parent, child) rows. How do you find the root?
option_a: It is the value that never appears as a child
option_b: It is the parent mentioned in the very first row of the input
option_c: It is the smallest value, because parents are created before children
option_d: It is the value that appears as a parent in exactly two rows
explanation: Every other node has exactly one parent, so it appears exactly once in the child column.

question: is_symmetric on the tree 1 2 2 # 3 # 3 (level order) returns?
option_a: true, because every level reads the same both ways
option_b: It crashes, because one of the 2s has no left child to compare
option_c: true, because both subtrees contain the same values in the same counts
option_d: false: both 3s are right children, so the halves are not mirrors
explanation: The levels are [1] [2 2] [3 3], but the shapes are not mirrored: mirror(left, right) compares left->right (3) with right->left (null).
